title: The Ringing Ears
briefing: Zoe, 16, spends three hours in the front row at a concert. On the way home her ears are ringing and voices sound muffled, as if through a pillow. By the next afternoon her hearing is normal again. Her friend, who stood at the back with earplugs in, is fine.
question: What did the sound do inside her ear — and why did it come back?

clues.title: Front row, three hours
clues.text: The sound meter app on her phone read about 110 dB by the speakers. Normal conversation is about 60 dB.
clues.shows: a huge amount of sound energy for a long time

clues.title: Ringing and muffled
clues.text: A steady high ring in both ears, and voices in the car sound distant and muffled.
clues.shows: the hearing cells sending a false signal and a weaker real one

clues.title: Back to normal by afternoon
clues.text: The ringing fades overnight; by the next afternoon voices sound sharp again.
clues.shows: that the cells recovered this time

clues.title: Earplugs at the back
clues.text: Her friend stood far from the speakers with earplugs in: no ringing, no muffling.
clues.shows: that less sound energy reaching the ear means no effect

hypotheses.text: She has water stuck in her ears.
hypotheses.flaw: Water would feel wet and shift when she tilts her head; it does not ring, and it would not depend on how loud the concert was.

hypotheses.text: Loud sound bent the tiny hair cells in her inner ear too hard for too long; they tired and sent a false 'ringing' signal while hearing less of the real one, then recovered overnight.
She shouted along too much and strained her ears.
hypotheses.flaw: Shouting strains the throat, not the ears — and her friend sang along just as loudly without any ringing.

hypotheses.text: The ringing is just in her imagination after the excitement.
hypotheses.flaw: Imagination does not make real voices sound muffled, and it does not vanish for the friend who wore earplugs.

prediction.prompt: Zoe listens for three hours. As the loudness rises — from conversation level up to front-row concert level — what happens to how tired her inner-ear hair cells get?

second.question: If she listens twice as long at the same loudness, what happens to the fatigue?

concepts.label: loud = far more energy
concepts.hint: What does 110 dB mean compared with 60?

concepts.label: hair cells in the inner ear
concepts.hint: What inside the ear actually turns sound into a signal?

concepts.label: bent too hard, they tire
concepts.hint: What happens to those cells under three hours of loud sound?

concepts.label: false signal = ringing
concepts.hint: What do tired hair cells send to the brain?

concepts.label: recovered this time
concepts.hint: Why was her hearing normal the next afternoon — and what does 'this time' hint at?

transfer.context: Tariq uses earbuds at full volume for his whole two-hour commute every day. Lately he turns the TV up louder than anyone else in the house.
options: The TV speakers are wearing out.
Hours of loud sound every day are tiring his inner-ear hair cells faster than they can recover, so quieter sounds are getting harder to hear.
He is distracted by his phone.
His ears are blocked with wax.
transfer.retryHint: Loud, for a long time, every day — which of Zoe's clues was about the dose of sound?
transfer.explanation: Zoe's hair cells got one big dose and had a day to recover. Tariq's get a big dose every day with no rest in between, so the fatigue does not clear — and the first sign is needing everything louder. Volume and time both count, and so do breaks.

takeaway: Hearing runs on tiny hair cells that bend with sound. Loud sound bends them too hard; ringing afterwards is their complaint. Give them a break and they recover — this time. Volume, time and rest all matter.
